overview: Separately catalogued skulls, limb bones and teeth support an aquatic-wading interpretation and a raoellid sister placement to Cetacea in the published analysis.

ecology.diet: Diet unresolved; stable isotopes constrain water use more directly than food choice
ecology.habitat: Aquatic or riparian use inferred from bone density and isotopes
ecology.locomotion: Wading interpretation inferred; no associated skeleton preserves a complete gait
ecology.guild: Aquatic-wading ecological interpretation with diet unresolved

evidenceSummary: The material is a disarticulated bone-bed sample, not one skeleton; aquatic ecology and sister placement are inferences, and Indohyus is neither crown Cetacea nor a demonstrated ancestor.

overview: Partial skeleton H-GSP 18507 combines large weight-bearing limbs with vertebral and hind-limb anatomy used to model amphibious swimming.

ecology.diet: Aquatic predation inferred from teeth and skull; prey not directly observed
ecology.habitat: Amphibious use inferred from anatomy and formation context
ecology.locomotion: Dorsoventral swimming and land movement are functional models
ecology.bodySize: Large-bodied early cetacean represented by a partial skeleton

traits: Substantial weight-bearing fore- and hind limbs
Vertebral and limb mosaic used in locomotor comparison
evidenceSummary: The holotype directly records an amphibious anatomical mosaic; otter-like swimming and sea-lion-like land movement are analogue-based models, not observed behaviour or ancestry.

overview: Holotype CGM 60584 combines a long posterior trunk, unfused sacrals, no weight-bearing sacroiliac joint and reduced limbs in a model of increasing tail propulsion.

ecology.diet: Marine predation inferred from cetacean dentition; prey not directly preserved
ecology.locomotion: Mid-body and tail undulation inferred; tail fluke not preserved
ecology.bodySize: Large protocetid represented by substantial associated remains

traits: Unfused sacrals without a weight-bearing sacroiliac joint
Reduced limbs and no securely preserved tail fluke
evidenceSummary: Associated material documents the locomotor anatomy, but age placement straddles competing stratigraphic interpretations and tail-driven swimming remains a model rather than observed performance.
